extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in arts/culture, comedy, censorship and Indian politics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit criteria about what makes stand-up comedy legally or socially risky in contemporary India — topics, performer identity, complainant/political influence, and enforcement mechanisms. Useful for comedians, advocates, or analysts assessing risk and likely reactions to political/religious satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topics considered sensitive
rubrics_metrics.description: Performances including jokes on religious riots, the controversial citizenship law, police brutality against students and the ongoing farmers' protest, and jokes about Hindu deities or political figures (eg. Amit Shah, Narendra Modi) are treated as 'sensitive'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists these topics as ones that have led to legal action or threats; comedians who address them face heightened risk of complaint, arrest, trolling, or demands for apology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alleged insult to religious deities as basis for legal action
rubrics_metrics.description: Police and complainants often allege 'objectionable comments' or 'insulting Hindu deities' at comedy events as the basis for registering offences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such allegations have been used to arrest performers even when the material was not actually performed in front of the complained-about audience (see 'insulted Hindu gods' claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal liability based on intention ('going to' crack jokes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities in Faruqui's case claimed he was liable not for jokes he told but for jokes he was 'going to' crack — effectively charging on a claimed intention or hypothetical allegation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece highlights criticism that police registered an offence 'merely on the basis of presumption' without evidence the performer actually made the remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement/evidence standard for 'deliberately intending to outrage religious feelings'
rubrics_metrics.description: To sustain charges under laws about outraging religious feelings, the prosecution must show evidence that the performer 'deliberately intending to outrage religious feelings'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faruqui's lawyer says police 'have failed to produce any evidence in court' of such intent; the article presents this as a central legal deficiency in the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complainant's political connections as a risk factor
rubrics_metrics.description: When complainants are politically connected (eg. 'the son of a BJP legislator and former minister'), cases may be perceived as driven by political pressure or influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes claims that complaints may be filed due to political influence and also contains denials from party officials; political connection is presented as a factor affecting the dynamics of complaints and investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vigilante/mob interruption and physical harassment as enforcement mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups such as the Hind Rakshak Sangathan can heckle, interrupt shows and hand performers over to police; performers may be 'roughed up' and detained by vigilantes prior to formal legal processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents how mob action precipitated arrests and how vigilante groups function as extra-legal enforcers of censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrospective policing of past content ('old videos dug up')
rubrics_metrics.description: Past online videos or old performances are frequently recovered and used as the basis for complaints or public outrage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several comedians had old material presented as evidence or examples (eg. Radhika Vaz, Agrima Joshua), increasing long-term risk from archived digital content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-judicial/civil pressure: threats, trolling, and demands for apology
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedians face online trolling, harassment, sexual-threats, and public pressure that can force cancellations or public apologies (eg. threats to Agrima Joshua; forced apology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such social pressures often produce self-censorship or reputational harm independent of legal outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal legal notices and contempt/show-cause processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedians and cartoonists may be served show-cause notices or contempt proceedings (eg. Kunal Kamra, Rachita Taneja) as a formal legal mechanism to challenge or punish perceived insults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These formal processes can be initiated by complaints even when the conduct is framed as political satire or criticism of institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry-level response and self-censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Many established comedians 'steer clear of political satire or commenting on religious groups' to avoid losing fans or inviting ire; the wider comedy industry often remains quiet when peers are targeted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article frames this as a protective practice: avoidance of sensitive topics reduces immediate risk but limits political satire and critical speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconsistent official statements and procedural lapses by police
rubrics_metrics.description: Police statements can be inconsistent (eg. claiming 'enough evidence' then saying the jokes were not made) and procedural failures occur (eg. failing to submit the case diary leading to adjourned hearings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such inconsistencies and lapses are presented as undermining the legitimacy of prosecutions and as grounds for defence claims of politically motivated or presumption-based arrests.
